screenings.title: Extreme Prejudice
screenings.description: Nick Nolte reteamed with his 48 Hrs. director Hill to portray grimly stoical Texas Ranger Jack Benteen, drawn into a border war with a Lonestar State expat, Cash Bailey (Powers Boothe), who has set up a lucrative drug trafficking operation on the south side of the Rio Grande and who just happens to be Benteen’s high school buddy—for good measure, both men are besotted with the same woman, played by María Conchita Alonso. Its cast filled out with a murderer’s row of ’80s action character actors (Clancy Brown, William Forsythe, Michael Ironside), Extreme Prejudice is a muscular modern-day Western that, in its apocalyptic shootout finale, offers more than a slight tip of the Stetson to the then-recently deceased Sam Peckinpah.

screenings.title: Before Sunrise
screenings.description: Linklater’s ongoing, decades-spanning story of a love affair through its many ups and downs begins here, with a chance encounter on a train between Ethan Hawke and Julie Delpy, the American Jesse and the French Céline, who together will pass a day and night in Vienna full of spirited, sparkling conversation and a slowly dawning attraction, all depicted with an ambling, uninflected naturalism. A wistful, winning, and quietly impassioned portrait of young love as it begins to bloom.

screenings.title: The Hole [Newly Struck 35mm Print]
screenings.description: It’s the close of the millennium and Taipei has emptied out with the onset of a mysterious virus, but The Man Upstairs (Lee Kang-sheng) and The Woman Downstairs (Yang Kuei-mei) lag behind among the ruins, where it doesn’t seem like there’s really much world to end, but maybe a last chance at communication through a breach between their apartments that slowly widens through Tsai’s downbeat, glum-funny dystopian masterpiece. Tsai's beloved film returns to Metrograph for a weeklong run on a newly struck 35mm print, approved by Tsai himself.

screenings.title: Europa
screenings.description: Also known as Zentropa, by any name von Trier’s film is a technical tour de force, its use of superimpositions and rear projection in layered widescreen compositions and expressionistic set design making for an orgy of formal flair unlike most anything else in cinema. In the immediate aftermath of World War II, idealistic young German American Leo Kessler (Jean-Marc Barr), who’s taken a job in US-occupied Deutschland as a conductor for the Zentropa railway company, finds himself caught up with a mysterious woman (Barbara Sukowa), “Werwolf” terrorists not reconciled to the postwar order, and a struggle for the future of a war-torn nation.

screenings.title: Good Time
screenings.description: A relentless, breakneck, candy-colored chase through the heart of Queens and Nassau County, the Safdies’ long, dark night of the soul thriller follows ne’er-do-well punk grifter “Connie” Nikas (Robert Pattinson) as he scrambles to spring brother Nick (Benny Safdie) from the clink after a bank job gone awry, finding himself embroiled in one botched scheme after another in the course of a sleepless night that takes him to sugar mama Jennifer Jason Leigh, through an Adventureland dark ride, and to the limits of endurance. A mesmerizing, frantic performance by Pattinson, in a harrowing work of bridge-and-tunnel psychedelia.

screenings.title: Angel Heart
screenings.description: An unusually explicit erotic thriller with more than a touch of the supernatural, Parker’s brazenly baroque adaptation of William Hjortsberg’s novel Falling Angel stars Mickey Rourke at his most beautiful as a private eye in Robert Wagner–era New York City who, hired onto a missing person case by a sinister client going by the name “Louis Cyphre” (Robert De Niro, shelling a hard-boiled egg with relish), lights out for New Orleans, where his investigation will expose him to brutal ritual murders, back-alley gumbo huts, and the considerable charms of the seductive Epiphany Proudfoot (Lisa Bonet, on a break from The Cosby Show and zestily slumming it up). “An exuberant exercise in style… Parker and his actors have fun taking it to the limit.” —Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

screenings.title: Tampopo
screenings.description: Japanese milk-truck drivers (Tsutomu Yamazaki and Ken Watanabe) team up with the owner of a run-down roadside food stall (Nobuko Miyamoto, in the title role) to help her kick up her noodle-making game a notch in Itami’s brash, bawdy, knee-slapping “ramen Western,” a paean to the simple pleasures to be found at the kitchen table and in the boudoir.

screenings.title: La Haine
screenings.description: A cinematic Molotov cocktail that was the first onscreen description of life (and death) in Paris’s banlieue housing projects that many French filmgoers had ever seen, La Haine depicts three armed and angry slum kids—Vincent Cassel, Hubert Koundé, and Saïd Taghmaoui—who, following days of rioting after the police’s savage beating of a young man, hit the city streets like ticking time bombs. A breakneck Steadicam journey through the concrete jungles of the suburbs, given an almost lunar desolation by the film’s black-and-white photography, La Haine is a propulsive, volatile, and visceral landmark of ’90s French cinema.

screenings.title: Arabesque
screenings.description: Donen’s “slick and satisfying” [Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader] Technicolor confection of romance, intrigue, flamboyant op-art inspired photography, and swank décor stars Gregory Peck as an American expert in hieroglyphics sucked into a criminal plot while doing a stint at Oxford and a sultry and seductive Sophia Loren as the woman who comes to his rescue. Frustrated with the scattershot script he’d been handed, Donen turned his focus to audiovisual experimentation, with the resulting feature part spy movie sendup, part over-the-top cinematic spree.

screenings.title: El Topo
screenings.description: Chilean-born mime-turned-filmmaker Jodorowsky plays the title role in this acid Western staple of the midnight movies, strapping on the six-shooter as a lone gunfighter—his name means “The Mole” in Spanish—traveling across a psychedelic desert landscape on a quest to vanquish increasingly unusual villains while simultaneously confronting his own spiritual anguish and existential dread. A mind-melting trip through the doors of perception that counted John Lennon among its many acolytes, made up of “a phantasmagoric Mexican landscape laden with dead bunnies and burros, snarling hippie chicks, pregnant silences, buckets of blood, and guru-gunslingers.”—Manohla Dargis, The New York Times

screenings.title: Lebanon in Turmoil preceded by South Lebanon
screenings.description: Saab had aspired to attend film school in her youth, but eventually found her way into cinema via journalism. Her first nonfiction feature, begun shortly after the slaughter of some six thousand Palestinians by right-wing Christian Phalangists in April 1975, which would spark a 15-year Civil War, is an inquest into this atrocity, charting the chain of events that had led Lebanon to the point of tragic self-immolation. Preceded by South Lebanon: History of a Besieged Village, in which Saab documents joint Lebanese-Israeli assault on Hanine and Kfarchouba, two “Fatah Land” frontier villages peopled with Palestinians.

screenings.title: Linda Linda Linda
screenings.description: With their last high school concert only days away, bandmates Kei, Kyoko, and Nozomi’s hopes of taking the stage appear to be dashed when their lead singer quits the group, leaving them to hastily recruit a Korean exchange student with a limited grasp of Japanese (Bae Doona) and go into lockdown practice mode. Featuring the music of The Blue Hearts and Base Ball Bear as well as original instrumentals courtesy of Smashing Pumpkins’s James Iha, Yamashita’s newly restored, irresistibly charming, bumptious hangout movie, subject of a healthy cult following in Japan as well as abroad, is less concerned with “coming of age” than with taking shelter, with a few good friends, from the oncoming adult crash.

screenings.title: Claire's Knee
screenings.description: Shot in the environs of Lake Annecy, Claire’s Knee—the fifth entry in Rohmer’s series of Six Moral Tales—concerns a cultured, soon-to-be-wed diplomat (Jean-Claude Brialy) who develops a consuming obsession with the knee of an acquaintance’s daughter, a fetish which in Rohmer’s hands takes on the character of an almost religious quest. With the always wonderful Béatrice Romand, making her first appearance in Rohmer’s stock company.

screenings.title: 3 Women
screenings.description: Alongside his more touted multi-character panoramas, Altman also had a fondness for small-scale dramas investigating the complexities of female psychology, and of these none is greater than the ineffable 3 Women, which finds Shelley Duvall, Sissy Spacek, and Janice Rule thrown together at a health spa in the California desert that caters to the elderly. As time passes, personas become increasingly permeable, and the proceedings feel like something conceived in a dream—which, indeed, the movie was!

screenings.title: Jacob's Ladder
screenings.description: Having proven himself a reliable hitmaker through the 1980s with Flashdance, 9½ Weeks, and Fatal Attraction, Lyne took an excursion into troubling new territory with this headlong plunge into the damaged psyche of Vietnam veteran Jacob Singer (Tim Robbins) who, haunted by his wartime experience and the death of a son, finds his drab daily life in c. 1975 New York City increasingly infringed on by nightmarish hallucinations—disturbing visions that suggest something more than run-of-the-mill PTSD. A nerve-fraying, phantasmagoric, wholly immersive waking nightmare that dangles its protagonist—and we, the audience—over a yawning abyss of horror. “Both a highly effective stream-of-consciousness puzzle thriller offering the viewer not one but many ‘solutions’ and an emotionally persuasive statement about the plight of many American vets.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Happy Together
screenings.description: Hong Kong cinema superstars Tony Leung and Leslie Cheung play a pair of lovers living out the waning days of their relationship as expatriates in Buenos Aires. Lusty tango bars, the salsa music of the La Boca sidewalks, and a hypnotic visit to the nearby Iguazu Falls give further dimension to the tensions growing between the two. Winner of the Best Director prize at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, Wong’s Happy Together is a stunning display of filmmaking style and a touching story of love on the brink of dissolution.

screenings.title: The Bakery Girl of Monceau + Suzanne's Career
screenings.description: Though rightfully an international arthouse phenomenon, Rohmer’s Moral Tales are remarkable in just how little they scream for attention, notable for their modesty of scale and their dedication to delicate observation rather than anything resembling firebrand provocation. The first two entries in the series are perfect instances of this: in The Bakery Girl of Monceau, a law student (a young Barbet Schroeder) flirts brazenly with the title character while brooding over his romantic failure with another girl; in Suzanne’s Career, in which two young men, a woman-shy introvert and a self-styled Don Juan, get mixed up with—and, in their individual ways, misuse—independent minded Catherine Sée, only to find their egos far more fragile than hers. Not exactly “high concept” stuff on the page, but on the screen… an abundance.

screenings.title: My Night at Maud's
screenings.description: Rohmer’s first feature-length entry in his “Six Moral Tales” series (following The Bakery Girl of Monceau and Suzanne’s Career) stars Jean-Louis Trintignant as a conscientious Catholic bachelor who is sorely tempted when he meets charming divorcée Françoise Fabian. Néstor Almendros’s black-and-white photography crystallizes the atmosphere of a damp Christmastime in mid-1960s central France while Rohmer exactingly depicts middle-class morals buckling under pressure as the sexual revolution arrives in the provinces.

screenings.title: Aferim!
screenings.description: Jude won Best Director from a Berlin jury for this, his third feature, a meticulously detailed, ribald evocation of 19th-century Romania evoking Cervantes and Rabelais as well as the American horse opera, and shot in tactilely textured black and white, following a blundering constable (Teodor Corban) and his weedy son as they trail a fugitive—a runaway Roma slave accused of rape by a grandee living in the cop’s jurisdiction—across the countryside of Wallachia. “Combine[s] the best pleasures of historical romp, road movie, and Western… A rich plundering of the language and prejudices of its time that makes you gasp and laugh despite yourself.” —Sight & Sound

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: Multihyphenate artists Barki and Bennani’s playful animation/live-action hybrid film à clef offers up a delightfully idiosyncratic look at the travails of the queer expat artist. The title character here is imagined as an anthropomorphic jackal inhabiting a New York City filled with other like critters, a young filmmaker simultaneously dealing with creative crises, her rocky relationship with her mother back in Casablanca, and the pleasures and perils of sex in the city. Drawing on real phone calls and myriad other correspondences, with voice talent courtesy of the directing duo’s friends and family members, this lay-it-on-the-line autofiction is at once startlingly light on its feet and densely layered with insight, not least into the feelings that come of shakily straddling two cultures while belonging fully to neither.

screenings.title: My Heart Is That Eternal Rose
screenings.description: Tam, perhaps the Hong Kong New Wave’s most daring cine-modernist and a crucial influence on Wong Kar-wai, teams with DP Christopher Doyle for a high-style “heroic bloodshed” melodrama starring Tony Leung Chiu-Wai, Kenny Bee, and Joey Wong as three friends bound together by ties both criminal and romantic. With shamelessly pulpy plotting, a synth-heavy score, luxuriously expressionistic imagery, and a climactic bloodbath for the ages, My Heart Is That Eternal Rose exists somewhere at the intersection between Wong’s cinema of longing and John Woo’s cinema of wrathful vengeance. One of the unheralded masterworks of Hong Kong filmmaking.

screenings.title: Basic Instinct
screenings.description: The film that made a star of Sharon Stone, seen to good effect in Verhoeven’s previous Carolco production, Total Recall, and that also provided the studio a succès de scandale windfall. Perfectly poised as she negotiates her way through the most infamous police station interrogation scene in cinema, Stone’s pulp novelist-and-suspected ice pick murderess Catherine Trammell is a blonde ice queen à la Hitchcock who begins to melt in the arms of besotted SFPD Detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas)—or does she only appear to? A work of carnivorous carnality that moves with prowling panther sleekness, its career-best Jerry Goldsmith score adding immeasurably to the undercurrent of imminent danger.

screenings.title: Possession
screenings.description: Easily the most harrowing divorce drama ever made, Zuławski’s one-of-a-kind genre pastiche has spy Sam Neill returning to his Berlin home from a mission abroad to discover that wife Isabelle Adjani wants suddenly to split up. Launching an investigation into the reasons for her ever-more-alarming behavior, he discovers a truth more sinister (and nauseating) than his wildest suspicions, as Zuławski’s highly-choreographed cinematic delirium and Andrzej Korzyński’s pulsating score push things light years past over-the-top. Adjani won a César for her performance, one of the most grueling ever caught on film, though later reflected that the palpable ordeal she put herself through on the movie was nearly enough to make her leave acting behind.

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Wake in Fright
screenings.description: It’s the eve of the Christmas holiday, and polite, young middle-class schoolteacher John Grant (Gary Bond), tied to a position at a tiny township in the outback, is on his way to Sydney to see his girlfriend by way of a stopoff in the grubby mining burg Bundanyabba (“The Yabba” to locals) when he pops into the pub for a drink… Five days of debauchery with local degenerates Donald Pleasence and Chips Rafferty later, the fresh-faced Grant has been replaced by a desperate, unshaven, beer-and-booze-pickled maniac, acquainted with species of depravity he could scarcely have imagined a week ago, and with the barbaric rites of the bush. A furious fever dream from Canuck director Kotcheff, who knew a thing or two about chronic self-degradation as practiced in far-flung outposts of the British Commonwealth, and one of the greatest of Australian films.

screenings.title: Chocolat
screenings.description: After years of honing her craft as assistant director for the likes of Jim Jarmusch and Wim Wenders, Denis emerged as a filmmaker with a distinct and fully-formed sense of her art in this, her sensual and infinitely sensitive semi-autobiographical feature debut, drawing on memories of a childhood spent in French-occupied Africa. In Cameroon, civil servant François Cluzet comes and goes on his appointed rounds, while his young daughter and neglected wife (Giulia Boschi) gravitate ever closer to their house servant, Protée (Isaach de Bankolé) in his absence, and the murmurs of anti-colonial resistance increase in vehemence away from eavesdropping whites. “Some kind of miniature classic.”—Vincent Canby, The New York Times

screenings.title: Conversation Piece
screenings.description: Burt Lancaster reunited with his The Leopard director for Visconti’s penultimate film, an elegant odd-couple chamber drama in which the leonine “Boit” plays a graying American intellectual immured from the modern world in his Roman palazzo—until, that is, his fortress of solitude is invaded by a pushy Marquise (Silvana Mangano) who browbears him into renting her his unused top floor to be used as a gilded cage for her boytoy, Konrad (Helmut Berger), a ’68 activist turned gigolo to the gentry, who interrupts the old man’s bedtime Mozart with Italopop and nude pot parties. Best known for his work in the epic vein, Visconti here renders verbal close-combat every bit as thrilling as any dispatch from the battlefields of Europe.

screenings.title: American Movie
screenings.description: The hit of the 1999 Sundance Film Festival, American Movie is the hilarious and intense story of one man’s obsession to make movies. Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, is a long way from Hollywood, but Mark Borchardt has a dream. Armed with a driving ambition and nothing to lose, the fast-talking Borchardt enlists friends, local thespians and unwilling family members to help him finish his no-budget horror film, Coven. The camera doesn’t flinch as it captures every emotional crisis and financial pitfall in his two-year odyssey. What emerges is a bizarre, yet surprisingly heartfelt, documentary portrait of a true American character.

screenings.title: Paranoid Park
screenings.description: Adapting Blake Nelson’s Y.A. novel of the same name, Van Sant renders the youth gathering place of the skate park a voluptuous dreamscape with the help of cinematographers Chris Doyle and Rain Kathy Li. Teenaged skate rat Alex—Gabe Nevins, leading a largely amateur cast recruited via MySpace—finds himself a prime suspect in the death of a security guard, silently carrying a crushing burden of knowledge through his daily rounds, a contrast to the gravity-defying liberation he finds carving it up at “Paranoid Park.”

screenings.title: The Fountain | 2006 Movies
screenings.description: As a modern-day scientist, Tommy is struggling with mortality, desperately searching for the medical breakthrough that will save the life of his cancer-stricken wife, Izzi.

screenings.title: Collateral
screenings.description: Los Angeles cabbie Max Durocher (Jamie Foxx) is in for the toughest fare of his working life when he picks up one Vincent (Tom Cruise, natty in charcoal gray sharkskin suit), a jazz enthusiast and professional hitman who quite firmly insists that his driver accompany him on his evening’s rounds, leaving a trail of bodies in his wake. Shooting LA exteriors after dark with a then-state-of-the-art Sony F-900 digital camera, Mann gave his film a wholly distinctive texture—combining expressionistic smear with a new ability to pick up detail that would be lost on celluloid—and initiated a quiet revolution in low-light cinematography. A drum-tight character-based thriller, and the only film in which you can see Tom Cruise saying: “Yo, homie… Is that my briefcase?”

screenings.title: The Milk of Sorrow
screenings.description: Winner of the Golden Bear at the 59th Berlin International Film Festival, Llosa’s formidable sophomore feature focuses on Fausta (Magaly Solier, in a performance nearly free of dialogue), the only daughter of an aged Indigenous Peruvian woman who, following her mother’s death, must negotiate arrangements for her burial as well as negotiate the smothering legacy of trauma that her parent, horribly misused during the Shining Path terrorist insurgencies of the 1980s and ’90s, has left behind with her child even after herself departing this mortal coil. “Littered with unforgettable images of incongruity, destruction, and, finally, healing” [The Village Voice], The Milk of Sorrow is an exquisitely shot study in inherited injury guarded like a precious heirloom, a work of tragic magic realism.

screenings.title: In the Glow of Darkness + Q&A
screenings.description: With the beating-heart-DIY spirit of George Kuchar and densely layered multimedia frenzy of Ryan Trecartin, L.A.-based filmmaker Tucker Bennett creates a gonzo, yet entirely plausible, sci-fi vision of our near future. In his fifth feature, Bennett melds a sincere love of ‘90s direct-to-video aesthetics and bygone blogosphere eras with a creative use of generative AI to create a kaleidoscopic, chronically-online cyberpunk-noir. With endless creativity and aesthetic integrity, Bennett lampoons and celebrates the myriad sub-cultures that populate today’s internet, betting that, in our post-ironic content-slop world, he can still stun his audience.

screenings.title: Hannibal
screenings.description: Hopkins reprises his role from 1991’s The Silence of the Lambs as psychiatrist-turned-cannibal serial killer Hannibal Lecter in Scott’s follow-up, a gristly fairy tale that finds FBI special agent Clarice Starling (Julianne Moore, ably taking on the role originated by Jodie Foster) racing against time to find to catch up with her old foil before he’s located by Mason R. Verger (Gary Oldman), a sadistic scion of enormous wealth who, after years earlier being grotesquely mutilated by Lecter, has dedicated the entirety of his power and influence towards a terrible and extravagant dream of vengeance. Unidentified in promotional materials and unbilled until the film’s closing credits, wholly unrecognizable under a prosthetic mask, and stripped of almost every expressive tool an actor traditionally relies upon to practice their craft, Oldman offers up an indelible portrayal of utter and absolute human corruption.

screenings.title: Scene of the Crime
screenings.description: One of seven collaborations between Téchiné and Catherine Deneuve, Scene of the Crime is a study of domestic discontent wearing the trappings of a boilerplate thriller, its action set into motion when a disconsolate 13-year-old boy runs across a fugitive criminal (Wadeck Stanczak) while loitering in a village cemetery, an encounter that will have immense repercussions for his woebegone mother, Lili (Deneuve), her manipulative estranged husband (Victor Lanoux), and Lili’s own overbearing mother (Danielle Darrieux, César nominated for her work here.) “The crux of the film is the mother-son relationship, and it is drawn in painful accuracy… An imaginatively structured, highly cinematic experience in which we watch with detachment the workings of fate unravel with a swift yet oddly calm inevitability.” —Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Jimmy
screenings.description: Shot in dreamy 16mm black and white, Yasshadai Owens’ debut feature Jimmy offers an intimate, speculative portrait of what a young James Baldwin may have experienced during his first trip to Paris in 1948. (credit: Toronto International Film Festival)

screenings.title: The Big Cheese
screenings.description: A scrappy team of eccentric American cheesemongers defies tradition to take on the world’s top cheese masters at the Mondial du Fromage, battling cultural clashes, personal struggles, and melting cheese in pursuit of respect, redemption, and a historic victory.

screenings.title: A Child of My Own
screenings.description: This new hybrid documentary from the Oscar-nominated director of The Mole Agent and The Eternal Memory follows the shocking tale of a woman desperate for a baby. Burdened by family and societal expectations, she fakes a pregnancy and gets tangled up in a crime.

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

screenings.title: CatVideoFest 2026
screenings.description: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CATVIDEOFEST 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations and shelters alike — a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need.

screenings.title: Wild Inside
screenings.description: Also playing: the 14-minute documentary short DREAM OF BIRDS screens with the 11:00am shows of WILD INSIDE Friday, July 31-Thursday August 6 only. Following a unique study led by Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin, DREAM OF BIRDS playfully explores the mystery of music through the mathematical patterns behind birdsong, and how our lives and relationships are rhythmically organized.

screenings.title: CatVideoFest 2026
screenings.description: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CatVideoFest 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations and shelters alike — a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need. Proceeds from Nitehawk shows will go to Sean Casey Animal Shelter.

screenings.title: Good Morning
screenings.description: Two brothers in a modern Japanese suburb go on strike to bring their parents to their knees and achieve their cherished dream: owning a television set for watching sumo matches. While borrowing from his own classic I Was Born, But… (1932), Ozu turns in a decidedly contemporary, family-friendly satire of a pop-culture colonized country seen in lively Agfacolor, which also functions as the single best showcase for the master’s fondness for fart jokes.

screenings.title: Le amiche
screenings.description: Perhaps the first of Antonioni’s films to give a clear indication of the direction of his mature style, this adaptation of Cesare Pavese’s Among Women Only finds glamorous Eleonora Rossi Drago returning to her hometown of Turin to open a branch of a fashion boutique, in the process taking up with the miserable, sniping local smart set and beginning an affair with architect’s assistant Franco Fabrizi. The air of bourgeois discontentment is thick, while the disquieting train station finale is the first of Antonioni’s great set pieces.

screenings.title: I Love Boosters
screenings.description: Starring Keke Palmer Naomi Ackie Taylour Paige Poppy Liu Eiza González LaKeith Stanfield Will Poulter Don Cheadle Demi Moore Jason Ritter Eric André

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: First Man
screenings.description: Dir. Damien Chazelle. 2018, 141 mins. U.S. DCP with Dolby Atmos. With Ryan Gosling, Claire Foy, Jason Clarke, Kyle Chandler, Corey Stoll, Christopher Abbott. Damien Chazelle followed up his Oscar win for La La Land with this surprising left turn, a brooding astronaut saga that plumbs genuine psychological depths in telling the life story of Neil Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon in 1969 as part of NASA’s long-gestating Gemini program. In a kind of flip side to his portrayal of goofball loneliness in Project Hail Mary, Gosling gives one of his best performances as a family man unable to bask in the fame and success of his world-changing mission, dealing with family tragedy. Featuring stellar supporting work from Claire Foy, First Man is a sophisticated and movingly human depiction of the years leading to the Apollo 11 mission, featuring a monumental orchestral score by Justin Hurwitz and tremendous visual effects authenticity supervised by Dune’s Paul Lambert. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth (ages 3–17) / discounted for MoMI members ($7–$11). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: A Child of My Own
screenings.description: This new hybrid documentary from the Oscar-nominated director of The Mole Agent and The Eternal Memory follows the shocking tale of a woman desperate for a baby. Burdened by family and societal expectations, she fakes a pregnancy and gets tangled up in a crime.

screenings.title: The Big Cheese
screenings.description: A scrappy team of eccentric American cheesemongers defies tradition to take on the world’s top cheese masters at the Mondial du Fromage, battling cultural clashes, personal struggles, and melting cheese in pursuit of respect, redemption, and a historic victory.

screenings.title: The Odyssey (35mm Screening)
screenings.description: Christopher Nolan’s next film, The Odyssey, is a mythic action epic shot across the world using brand new IMAX® film technology. The film brings Homer’s foundational saga to IMAX® film screens for the first time and opens in theaters everywhere on July 17, 2026.

screenings.title: Olmo
screenings.description: Olmo just wants to be a normal teenager and hang out with his best friend, but he must help care for his bedridden father. She may earn her piano back if she allows him to do certain things while she plays ; one black key for every lesson. The arrangement draws all three deeper and deeper into a complex emotional, sexual bond remarkable for its naive passion and frightening disregard for limits.

screenings.title: ∞ Infinity Day: Parallel Universes Explained!
screenings.description: Quantum mechanics explore how a particle can be superimposed into multiple states of being at the same time. When disturbed by observation or measurement, particles “choose” from one of many possible states and present just one. What are the implications of this choice? Its study is one of the foundations of the theory in physics underpinning exploration of parallel universes. Prepare to have your worldview expanded in this conversation led by quantum physicist Niccolo Bigagli, exploring the scientific underpinning of the multiverse, illustrated by favorite film clips. RSVP recommended. Seating is first come, first served. Special guests Niccolo Bigagli is a quantum physicist whose experiments span the study of quantum particles from their most fundamental properties as single entities to their behavior when many thousands are brought together. In his PhD, Niccolò observed for the first time a novel phase of matter, a Bose Einstein Condensate of dipolar molecules, where molecules act as a fascinating single body while still interacting amongst themselves. Currently, he is studying quantum networks, that is how to harness photons’ quantum mechanical nature to unlock new technology and new experimental capabilities. Niccolò also dabbles in film and photography, with a special interest in analog techniques. Open Worlds: Science is funded by Simons Foundation International and administered by the Simons Foundation’s Science, Society & Culture division.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: The Chaser
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from the gristly exploits of South Korean serial killer Yoo Young-chul, Na’s astonishingly assured directorial debut stars Ha Jung-woo as a sadistic killer, Ji Yeong-min, and Kim Yoon-seok as Joong-ho, an ex-detective with a checkered past now running a prostitution ring. After helplessly watching his stable of employees disappear and dwindle, Joong-ho sets out to find the sicko responsible—and in the course of a sleepless night of cat and mouse, finds he has to contend not only with the killer’s calculating intelligence and red herring misleads, but with an incompetent police force and a thicket of bureaucratic barriers that seem to have been erected with the specific purpose of allowing the guilty to get away clean. Winner of Best Actor, Best Film, and Best Director at Korea’s Grand Bell Awards, The Chaser is both a precision-tuned white-knuckle thriller and an agonized exploration of insoluble moral conundrums.

screenings.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey (70mm)
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1968, 149 mins (plus intermission). U.S. 70mm. With Keir Dullea, Gary Lockwood. As brilliantly engineered as the space program itself, Stanley Kubrick’s mysterious and profound sci-fi epic—“the ultimate trip”—is about nothing less than the beauty and the banality of civilization, blending cool satire, an elaborate vision of the future, and passages of avant-garde cinematic inventiveness. Set in a future that is already the past, 2001 envisions space travel as both hilariously routine and mind-bending, a journey to the infinite and beyond that forever changed the way we see the universe and cinema itself. As experienced on 70mm in MoMI’s Redstone Theater, Kubrick’s surreal masterwork still has the ability to conduct viewers to untold, unknowable realms of artistry and daring. screenings.title: The Flying Dutchman
screenings.description: “DEFA’s The Flying Dutchman is considered the first attempt to film a Wagner opera in its entirety, although, in point of fact, it too reworks the story to suit both the cinematic medium and the political viewpoint of the GDR. It was directed by opera director Joachim Herz, who, perhaps because it was his first (and only) film, opted to experiment with state-of-the-art sound and film techniques. Director Herz dramatically changes Wagner’s opera from one about a ghostly event to the reveries of a young woman named Senta who is infatuated with the story of the Flying Dutchman. To separate reality from Senta’s imagination, Mr. Herz uses two different film aspect ratios. Whenever we are watching Anna in the real world, the aspect ratio is [in 1.67:1]. When the film shifts to Senta’s dream world, the screen slowly opens up to the 2.35:1 dimensions of DEFA’s Totalvision (the same as Cinemascope). In other films that use multiple aspect ratios, the change in screen aspect is handled as edits, but Herz wanted these switches in perspective to flow like the film’s lush score. To do this required sophisticated in-camera techniques involving animation frames and an American Mitchell camera that accepted double reels. This process meant that everything had to be shot with the larger format while the animation frame was simultaneously running through the camera. That this worked at all is a testament to cinematographer Erich Gusko’s skill with a camera.” – Jim Morton

Hoberman, a combination of “super-grunt, Green Beret, hippie protester, VC guerilla, righteous outlaw [and] Hollywood Freedom Fighter.” Arriving in the town of Hope, Washington State, after paying his respects to an old army buddy who’s died from the lingering effects of Agent Orange exposure, Rambo is escorted to the city limits by hard-ass local sheriff Brian Dennehy who, with this slight, unwittingly lights the fuse on a human stick of dynamite. screenings.description: Moustapha AlassaneAN ADVENTURER’S HOMECOMING / RETOUR D’UN AVENTURIER1966, 34 min, 16mm-to-DCP. In Hausa and French with English subtitles.“Jimi flies back to his native village after a long absence and convinces his friends to become cowboys. Renamed Black Cooper, John Kelly, Breaker, Billy Walter, and Queen Christine, they steal horses, terrorize sheepherders, and brawl in the neighborhood saloon to the horror of the locals. Drawing maximum effects from an economy of means, Alassane’s brilliant comedy intertwines central modernization plots in West Africa and Europe after the war (a traveler’s return, the youth problem, the arrival of new technology) with the outlaw gang and frontier-town-under-attack narratives that were mainstays of the western genre. By stripping these stories of their conventional moral weight, he opens his film, ‘the first African western,’ to the widest scope of possible interpretations.” –Jamie Berthe & Sam Di IorioKevin Jerome EversonTEN FIVE IN THE GRASS2011, 32 min, Super-8mm-to-digital. Screening courtesy the artist and Picture Palace Pictures.“The black western richly provokes the mythology of the American West and the idea of film genre as a historiographic Imagineering by tacitly revealing how the narrative form has covertly borne a racial and cultural ideal. The genre’s classical themes of nation-building, the civilizing of savage lands, utopianism, and the discreteness of good and evil become refabulated as Everson draws attention to absences, disavowals, and the difference of a culture other than pale riders. Everson’s TEN FIVE IN THE GRASS examines the craft of the black cowboy. The film illustrates Everson’s interest in everyday intellect by observing the rituals of the grooming of horses, riding, and roping. The piece is set in a practice space in Natchez, Mississippi run by Fred Mayberry, a rancher and professional rodeo calf roper.” –Michael B. As they face an impossible choice between love and survival, they must decide if they want to build a family and chart a path to happiness in Lebanon, despite the tragedies ravaging the country. In Arabic with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Uncut Gems + Galaxies
screenings.description: From acclaimed filmmakers Josh and Benny Safdie comes an electrifying crime thriller about Howard Ratner (Adam Sandler), a charismatic New York City jeweler always on the lookout for the next big score. When he makes a series of high-stakes bets that could lead to the windfall of a lifetime, Howard must perform a precarious high-wire act, balancing business, family, and encroaching adversaries on all sides, in his relentless pursuit of the ultimate win.

screenings.title: I Want Your Sex
screenings.description: Elliot’s (Hoffman) fantasies come true when he lands a job with a renowned artist (Wilde).

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: The Invite
screenings.description: A dinner party spirals into unexpected places in this star-studded portrait of marriage.

screenings.title: Wild Inside
screenings.description: Also playing: the 14-minute documentary short DREAM OF BIRDS screens with the 11:00am shows of WILD INSIDE Friday, July 31-Thursday August 6 only. Following a unique study led by Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin, DREAM OF BIRDS playfully explores the mystery of music through the mathematical patterns behind birdsong, and how our lives and relationships are rhythmically organized.

screenings.title: Olmo
screenings.description: Olmo just wants to be a normal teenager and hang out with his best friend, but he must help care for his bedridden father. When Olmo gets invited to a party by his beautiful neighbor, he will do whatever he can to meet up with her while embarking on an adventure of mischief, laughs, and chaos. As the night unfolds, he may come to love the very place he’s spent so long trying to escape: his home. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Maddie's Secret
screenings.description: Tuesday, June 16 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early Wednesday, June 17 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early and Carla Lalli Friday, June 19 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by John Wilson Friday, June 19 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Brace Belden Friday, June 19 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Ivy Wolk Friday, June 10 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early Saturday, June 20 at 11:30: Q&A with John Early moderated by Julio Torres Saturday, June 20 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Theda Hammel Saturday, June 20 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Sarah Sherman Saturday, June 20 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Amy Sedaris Saturday, June 20 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Roller Junkies
screenings.description: Hollywood-sleaze auteur Jared Masters is an LA based, low budget filmmaker, creating an array of women-centric features inspired by VHS slashers and 60’s B-movies. His films represent a modern take on genre films, and have John Waters/Kuchar Brothers humor to them. Jared refers to himself as a modern cult filmmaker, occasionally starring in the films he makes. The three films selected are an introduction to his filmography, highlighting his taste for camp and self-aware humor, backed by a clear love for cinema. Masters works align with the Spectacle vision to highlight underrated, seldom-viewed filmmakers and late-night summer indies.

screenings.title: Millennium Mambo
screenings.description: A stylish and seductive submersion into the techno-scored neon nightlife of Taipei, Hou’s much-misunderstood marvel stars Shu Qi (The Assassin) as an aimless bar hostess drifting away from her blowhard boyfriend and towards Jack Kao’s suave, sensitive gangster. Structured as a flashback to the then-present from the then-future of 2011, it’s a transfixing trance-out of a movie, drenched in club lights, ecstatic endorphin-rush exhilaration, and a nagging undercurrent of ennui. Hou and longtime cinematographer Lee here break from their familiar pattern of elegantly composed long shot long takes to create something both more intimate and hectic, a film whose shallow-focus images, jittery camerawork, and cramped locations evoke both the claustrophobic character of Taiwan’s capital city and, in Lee’s words, “the feeling of youth.”

screenings.title: In the Mood for Love
screenings.description: Wong’s arthouse smash is the very simple tale of two people in early ’60s Hong Kong, Mr. Chow (Tony Leung Chiu-wai) and Mrs. Chen (Maggie Cheung), drawn to one another by the discovery that their spouses are getting together on the side. A little story, full of little details, all surrounding a love affair that isn’t really a love affair—but throbbing with huge, aching emotions that it can barely contain. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: ∞ Infinity Day: Short Films about Math
screenings.description: This selection of films showing the artists’ take on explorations of math range from simple counting through mind-boggling explanations of the vast and infinitesimal. Program runs 41 minutes. Pinball Number Count #8 Forest Follies Dir. Jeff Hale. 1977, 1 min. U.S. A mainstay of Sesame Street, this iconic animation series of the inside of a pinball machine features a super funky soundtrack and vocals from the Pointer Sisters. Number 8 in the series features unicycling bears and other forest animals. Sesame Street excerpts provided courtesy of Sesame Workshop. Numerosity Number 8 Dir. Jim Henson. 1969, 2 mins, U.S.. The 8th in the ‘”Baker numbers” series for Sesame Street features adults, puppies, and children counting to eight and culminates in the dramatic appearance of a clumsy baker. Courtesy of The Jim Henson Legacy. © Sesame Workshop The Dot and the Line: A Romance in Lower Mathematics Dir. Chuck Jones, co-dir. Maurice Noble. 1965, 10 mins. U.S. A straight blue line is hopelessly in love with a red dot. Based on a book by Norton Juster, author of The Phantom Tollbooth, the film is a more esoteric work from the legendary animation director Chuck Jones, one of the creators of Bugs Bunny and Wile E. Coyote for Looney Tunes. Symmetry Dirs. Charles and Ray Eames. 1961, 3 mins. U.S. One of five “Peep Shows” the iconic designers Charles and Ray Eames created for their IBM-sponsored exhibition, Mathematica, the film introduces the concept of various degrees of symmetry, giving viewers a “peep” of the mathematical concept. © 2026 Eames Office, LLC. All rights reserved. The King of 8 Dir. Jim Henson. 1970, 1 min. U.S. Masterfully created in stop-motion animation by Henson and Don Sahlin, the King of the Land of 8 tells about all the items that number 8 in a rhythmic song. Find the puppets from the film, created by Sahlin, on view in The Jim Henson Exhibition. Courtesy of The Jim Henson Legacy © Sesame Workshop Spheres Dirs. Norman McLaren and René Jodoin. 1969, 8 mins. Canada. In this three-part experiment in geometric abstraction, spheres with metallic reflections float and are propelled through space. Lustrously hand-painted stop-motion animation set to Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier, played by pianist Glenn Gould. Courtesy ONF/NFB Animation vs. Geometry Dir. Alan Becker. 2024, 9 mins. U.S. A yellow stick figure fights its way through an increasingly complex world of vicious angles and polygons. Powers of Ten and the Relative Size of Things in the Universe Dirs. Charles and Ray Eames. 1977, 9 mins. U.S. Investigating the idea of an exponential series, the film illustrates scale and the significance of adding a zero to a number. It begins with a couple picnicking in a park bordering Lake Michigan in Chicago. The journey steadily moves away from the couple, reaching the edge of the known universe, before reversing back down to the atomic level of the hand of the man napping on the picnic blanket. Original music score by Elmer Bernstein. © 2026 Eames Office, LLC. All rights reserved. RSVP recommended. Seating is first come, first served. Open Worlds: Science is funded by Simons Foundation International and administered by the Simons Foundation’s Science, Society & Culture division.

screenings.title: Blades of Glory
screenings.description: Two figure skating rivals are banned from the sport after a brawl over the gold medal. Joining forces, they find a loophole in the rules that allows them to skate again… as a pair!

screenings.title: Thief
screenings.description: Becoming closer to his dream of leading a normal life, a professional safecracker agrees to do a job for the mafia, who have other plans for him. Released in the US as Violent Streets, Michael Mann’s super influential minimalist neo-noir looks as authentic and original today as the day it did in 1981. Mann used real thieves as technical advisors on the film and that Tangerine Dream soundtrack is a joy. Donald Thorin’s moody and brilliant cinematography seals the deal.

screenings.description: Sat Aug 8: The Big Cheese Q&A w/dir. Sara Joe Wolansky & subject Adam Moskowitz, moderated by Josh Windsor, after the 7:35 sho

screenings.title: Gummo
screenings.description: Teen friends Tummler (Nick Sutton) and Solomon (Jacob Reynolds) navigate the ruins of a tiny, tornado-ravaged town in Ohio that is populated by the deformed, disturbed and perverted. When not gunning down stray cats for a few bucks, the boys pass their time getting stoned on household inhalants. Elsewhere, the mute Bunny Boy (Jacob Sewell) dons rabbit ears and is bullied by kids half his age, and sisters Dot (Chloe Sevigny) and Helen (Carisa Glucksman) dodge a pedophile.

screenings.title: Satan's Menagerie
screenings.description: Dr. Craymoor (co-writer Thomas V. Powers, doing his best hammy public-access-Vincent Price) is a paranormal talk show host who dabbles in the dark arts in pursuit of fame and riches. We’ll refrain from spoiling the (surprisingly convoluted) plot, but it involves, among other things, a Vietnam vet turned werewolf, a half-man half-amphibian who escapes from a carnival sideshow, and the disciples of a centuries old blood cult called the ‘Sons of Jeramin’.

screenings.title: Ghost in the Shell
screenings.description: “We follow Kusanagi on her hunt for The Puppet Master, a hacker who can access the ‘ghosts’, or souls, of ordinary citizens and carry out cyber-crimes by proxy. Now entirely synthetic, her original human body replaced and improved on piece by piece, Kusanagi is unsure whether her ghost still lingers in her man-made form: in the opening credits, her cybernetic form is assembled in a factory, and the haunting temple chant on the soundtrack makes the process look like a religious rite.

screenings.title: Jimmy
screenings.description: Shot in dreamy 16mm black and white, Yasshadai Owens’ debut feature Jimmy offers an intimate, speculative portrait of what a young James Baldwin may have experienced during his first trip to Paris in 1948. (credit: Toronto International Film Festival)

screenings.title: The Big Cheese
screenings.description: A scrappy team of eccentric American cheesemongers defies tradition to take on the world’s top cheese masters at the Mondial du Fromage, battling cultural clashes, personal struggles, and melting cheese in pursuit of respect, redemption, and a historic victory.

screenings.title: A Child of My Own
screenings.description: This new hybrid documentary from the Oscar-nominated director of The Mole Agent and The Eternal Memory follows the shocking tale of a woman desperate for a baby. Burdened by family and societal expectations, she fakes a pregnancy and gets tangled up in a crime.

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

A harsh but cautiously hopeful depiction of the lives of young Afro-French women, and the unique adversities they face.

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: The Odyssey (35mm Screening)
screenings.description: Christopher Nolan’s next film, The Odyssey, is a mythic action epic shot across the world using brand new IMAX® film technology. The film brings Homer’s foundational saga to IMAX® film screens for the first time and opens in theaters everywhere on July 17, 2026.

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: Henson Fan Appreciation Day: A Salute to Henson Fans (But Mostly ToughPigs)
screenings.description: If a frog sings in a swamp and no one’s around to hear him, does his banjo make a sound? Where would the Muppets be without their fans? Throughout Henson history, through movies and television shows and reboots and all those quiet moments in between, the fans have kept the spirit of Jim Henson alive. This August, Museum of the Moving Image will be paying tribute to those dedicated fans in the Muppet Theatre audience. That’s you!! To pay homage to the Henson fan community, Jim Henson Legacy President Craig Shemin will be in conversation with members of Muppet fan site ToughPigs.com (celebrating its 25th anniversary) and the admins of the Muppet Wiki. And as a “thank you” to all the dedicated fans, the event will feature a screening of a rare classic production from the Henson vaults! This event is for casual Henson fans, die-hard fanatics, and everyone in between! Whether you have fond memories of watching The Muppet Movie or if you’ve memorized every line of dialogue, MoMI salutes you! Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth (ages 3–17) / free for MoMI members at the Senior/Student level and above. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: Le amiche
screenings.description: Perhaps the first of Antonioni’s films to give a clear indication of the direction of his mature style, this adaptation of Cesare Pavese’s Among Women Only finds glamorous Eleonora Rossi Drago returning to her hometown of Turin to open a branch of a fashion boutique, in the process taking up with the miserable, sniping local smart set and beginning an affair with architect’s assistant Franco Fabrizi. The air of bourgeois discontentment is thick, while the disquieting train station finale is the first of Antonioni’s great set pieces.

screenings.title: Julian
screenings.description: Fleur and Julian fall madly in love and decide to get married in all countries where they, as two women, are allowed to do so. But after only four marriages, their journey comes to a painful and unexpected halt.

screenings.title: The Odyssey (DCP)
screenings.description: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

screenings.title: The Hole [Newly Struck 35mm Print]
screenings.description: It’s the close of the millennium and Taipei has emptied out with the onset of a mysterious virus, but The Man Upstairs (Lee Kang-sheng) and The Woman Downstairs (Yang Kuei-mei) lag behind among the ruins, where it doesn’t seem like there’s really much world to end, but maybe a last chance at communication through a breach between their apartments that slowly widens through Tsai’s downbeat, glum-funny dystopian masterpiece. Tsai's beloved film returns to Metrograph for a weeklong run on a newly struck 35mm print, approved by Tsai himself.

screenings.title: The Piano - New 4K Restoration
screenings.description: Ada – mute since birth – her nine year old daughter and her piano arrive to an arranged marriage in the remote bush of nineteenth century New Zealand. Of all her belongings her husband refuses to transport the piano and it is left behind on the beach. Unable to bear its certain destruction, Ada strikes a bargain with an illiterate tattooed neighbour. She may earn her piano back if she allows him to do certain things while she plays ; one black key for every lesson. The arrangement draws all three deeper and deeper into a complex emotional, sexual bond remarkable for its naive passion and frightening disregard for limits.

screenings.title: Amadeus (70mm)
screenings.description: Producer Paul Zaentz in person on August 9 Dir. Milos Forman. 1984, 160 mins. U.S./France. 70mm. With F. Murray Abraham, Tom Hulce, Elizabeth Berridge, Jeffrey Jones, Christine Ebersole, Simon Callow, Cynthia Nixon. Milos Forman’s thrilling, Best Picture–winning adaptation of Peter Shaffer’s play may be, without parallel, the greatest cinematic evocation of artistic jealousy, centering on the mythic rivalry between Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Antonio Salieri in 18th-century Vienna. Court composer for Emperor Joseph II, Salieri grows increasingly resentful of the ease with which the crass, childlike musician writes his works of astonishing beauty, leading to tragedy. Personifying the timeless, fruitless struggle between genius and mediocrity, Amadeus is a film of operatic force and keen wit, featuring brilliant performances by both Tom Hulce as Mozart and especially an Oscar-winning F. Murray Abraham as his envious competitor. Buy tickets for August 7 Buy tickets for August 9 Tickets: $25 / 25% discount for MoMI members. screenings.title: Blood Brunch
screenings.description: Calling all Bloodeaters, Love Butchers and Neon Maniacs! The lights go down, the screen lights up and every one of your senses is flooded with ghastly terror from beyond the fetid grave. Spend your Sundays drenched in blood and quivering in fear with a mystery movie—as in, we don’t tell you what we’re showing until you see the title on the screen—that is at least 20 years old.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: The Kid
screenings.description: Regarded as the Tramp’s first jump into feature films, this family-friendly six-reeler shows Chaplin at his most brilliant and most sentimental, plumbing memories of his own boyhood of almost Dickensian deprivation. The Tramp adopts an abandoned boy, played by soon-to-be-child-superstar Jackie Coogan, and fights against remarkable odds to keep the lad at his side. Gives us some of the most moving passages in Chaplin’s nakedly emotional filmography, including Charlie’s desperate search through city poorhouses for his missing charge, and the visualization of a poor boy’s imagining of heaven.

screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Sheep in the Box

screenings.title: Rebecca
screenings.description: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay again…” Hitchcock was still a newly arrived UK import when this gothic thriller/romance, based on the novel of the same title by Daphne du Maurier, took Outstanding Production (later “Best Picture”) honors at the Academy Awards. Joan Fontaine stars as a terribly self-conscious young woman, never identified by name, who becomes enamored with a saturnine, aristocratic widower, Maxim de Winter (Laurence Olivier, fresh from Wuthering Heights)—and, once she’s been taken as his bride, obsessed with his late wife’s phantom presence in their home on the Cornwall coast. A marvel of directorial assurance that turns the screws with poise and panache.

screenings.title: Olmo

When Olmo gets invited to a party by his beautiful neighbor, he will do whatever he can to meet up with her while embarking on an adventure of mischief, laughs, and chaos. As the night unfolds, he may come to love the very place he’s spent so long trying to escape: his home. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. screenings.title: Late Fame

Directed by Kent Jones (DIANE) from a witty, razor-sharp script by Samy Burch (MAY DECEMBER), LATE FAME is a funny, lively, poignant, and occasionally haunting New York story. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film 2025 96 MIN. USA MAGNOLIA PICTURES

screenings.title: Favorites of the Moon
screenings.description: Having relocated to France in 1982, Iosseliani wasted no time in showing the world he hadn’t left his singular gifts behind upon leaving Georgia, taking home the Special Jury Prize at the 41st Venice International Film Festival for this puckish panoramic comedy about dizzying reversals of fortune and everyday acts of larceny, petty and otherwise. Terrorists, chanteuses, antique dealers, police inspectors, street walkers, and street sweepers all have a part to play in this farcical fable located at the intersection of Dickens and Tati, which follows the circulation of two precious objects—a Limoges porcelain dinner service and a portrait of a Belle Époque–era aristocratic beauty—as they’re passed from one pair of hands to another, and up and down the socioeconomic hierarchy, in Paris’s 13th arrondissement. Co-written with regular Polanski collaborator Gérard Brach, and featuring a very fresh-faced Mathieu Amalric in his very first film role.

screenings.title: Highway Hypnosis
screenings.description: Between the years of 1974 to 1979, not long after Manson Family trials had concluded, enigmatic artist and connoisseur of fringe culture, John Aes-Nihil, embarked on a project to “re-stage” the events leading up to the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders as a series of faux home movies, based on the legend that the Family had at one point stolen camera equipment to document their actions. The resulting feature— which, coincidentally, premiered in 1984 at EZTV alongside HIGHWAY HYPNOSIS— truly lives up to its filmmaker’s namesake Aesthetic Nihilism: Shot entirely on Super8mm and completely silent save for an accompanying soundtrack mostly comprised of music made by the Family itself (plus a little Patty Duke for good measure). The film re-frames the Manson Family story as a first-person travelogue across Southern California, imbued with chillingly realistic detail as we bear (false) witness to one of the most notorious events of the American century.

screenings.description: Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela’s (Olivia Wilde) marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors (Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton) for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places. Have they reignited the spark or lit the match that burns it all down? A remake of the 2020 Spanish film The People Upstairs, Olivia Wilde’s star-studded take on a dinner party dramedy (written by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones) is a timely portrait of a modern marriage, teeming with wit, belly laughs, and a surprising poignancy.

As a child escapes from everyday daily life to the magic of a storybook, so, in the film, Beauty’s farm, with its Vermeer simplicity, fades in intensity as we are caught up in the Gustave Doré extravagance of the Beast’s enchanted landscape. In Christian Bérard’s makeup, Jean Marais is a magnificent Beast.” –Pauline KaelCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. screenings.title: Conversation Piece
screenings.description: Burt Lancaster reunited with his The Leopard director for Visconti’s penultimate film, an elegant odd-couple chamber drama in which the leonine “Boit” plays a graying American intellectual immured from the modern world in his Roman palazzo—until, that is, his fortress of solitude is invaded by a pushy Marquise (Silvana Mangano) who browbears him into renting her his unused top floor to be used as a gilded cage for her boytoy, Konrad (Helmut Berger), a ’68 activist turned gigolo to the gentry, who interrupts the old man’s bedtime Mozart with Italopop and nude pot parties. Best known for his work in the epic vein, Visconti here renders verbal close-combat every bit as thrilling as any dispatch from the battlefields of Europe.
