screenings.title: And Then There Was Light
screenings.description: The confrontation of a traditional rural/agrarian culture bound to the land and the cycles of the seasons and an urban/industrial society that has largely forgotten these ties, an abiding concern of Iosseliani’s cinema, plays out against a backdrop entirely new to his work in this fable-like homage to silent cinema, intertitles and all. In the village of Casamance in southern Senegal, home to the Jola people, life goes on much as it has since time immemorial, with its gossip-mongering, its local scandals, its rituals of field labor and midday meals—until, that is, new European machinery begins to arrive on the scene, its intended use: deforestation of the region and exploitation of its natural resources. “There is an interweaving, an interdependence, of real life and ancient poetry… The film’s texture is not raw, not naturalistic. In Africa, as in his native Georgia, [Iosseliani] enters into a kind of symbiosis with the ‘spirit’ of the country.” —Le Monde

screenings.title: Dread Beat an Blood
screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... An amazing snapshot of the time of the pre-Brixton riots... This is so relevant a movie. That’s what makes it so good.” – Gilles Peterson, BBC “A fascinating document of LKJ in his time and place, touring with the sound systems, strolling through the market and visiting Tulse Hill schools, vividly capturing black British culture in a country on the cusp of Thatcherism, just a few months before the Brixton uprising.” – Stephen Troussé, Uncut “An invaluable document of Brixton, an area that was already at the front lines of the anti-racist struggle, the streets in which people would soon rise up in rebellion. That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... He’s now celebrated as one of this country’s most influential cultural commentators.” – BBC “A revolutionary poet for our times.” – Jacobin “The Poet Laureate of Black Britain.” – Paul Gilroy “The roots of hip-hop run deep, and among the deepest branches remains Linton Kwesi Johnson, the Jamaican-born, British-raised poet, writer, and performer often hailed as the father of dub poetry.” – David Browne, Rolling Stone

screenings.title: The Chaser
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from the gristly exploits of South Korean serial killer Yoo Young-chul, Na’s astonishingly assured directorial debut stars Ha Jung-woo as a sadistic killer, Ji Yeong-min, and Kim Yoon-seok as Joong-ho, an ex-detective with a checkered past now running a prostitution ring. After helplessly watching his stable of employees disappear and dwindle, Joong-ho sets out to find the sicko responsible—and in the course of a sleepless night of cat and mouse, finds he has to contend not only with the killer’s calculating intelligence and red herring misleads, but with an incompetent police force and a thicket of bureaucratic barriers that seem to have been erected with the specific purpose of allowing the guilty to get away clean. Winner of Best Actor, Best Film, and Best Director at Korea’s Grand Bell Awards, The Chaser is both a precision-tuned white-knuckle thriller and an agonized exploration of insoluble moral conundrums.

screenings.description: One of seven collaborations between Téchiné and Catherine Deneuve, Scene of the Crime is a study of domestic discontent wearing the trappings of a boilerplate thriller, its action set into motion when a disconsolate 13-year-old boy runs across a fugitive criminal (Wadeck Stanczak) while loitering in a village cemetery, an encounter that will have immense repercussions for his woebegone mother, Lili (Deneuve), her manipulative estranged husband (Victor Lanoux), and Lili’s own overbearing mother (Danielle Darrieux, César nominated for her work here.) “The crux of the film is the mother-son relationship, and it is drawn in painful accuracy… An imaginatively structured, highly cinematic experience in which we watch with detachment the workings of fate unravel with a swift yet oddly calm inevitability.” —Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: Multihyphenate artists Barki and Bennani’s playful animation/live-action hybrid film à clef offers up a delightfully idiosyncratic look at the travails of the queer expat artist. The title character here is imagined as an anthropomorphic jackal inhabiting a New York City filled with other like critters, a young filmmaker simultaneously dealing with creative crises, her rocky relationship with her mother back in Casablanca, and the pleasures and perils of sex in the city. Drawing on real phone calls and myriad other correspondences, with voice talent courtesy of the directing duo’s friends and family members, this lay-it-on-the-line autofiction is at once startlingly light on its feet and densely layered with insight, not least into the feelings that come of shakily straddling two cultures while belonging fully to neither.

screenings.title: Toute une nuit
screenings.description: Emotions boil over and thunder rolls during one oppressively humid summer night in Brussels in Akerman’s tender and melancholy film of brief encounters, furtive embraces, nocturnal despair, yearning vigils, and pregnant silences. A string of self-contained vignettes, precisely composed and parsimonious in use of dialogue, their abiding air of tension occasionally rent by cloudbursts of frenzied feeling, Toute une nuit may be regarded, like the filmmaker’s News from Home, as an inimitable twist on the “city symphony” genre, laying its scenes in the bars, cafes, and streets of Akerman’s hometown. “A comédie sentimentale treated as a choreographed dance.” —Cahiers du Cinéma

screenings.description: The third entry in Rohmer’s Six Moral Tales series, in which cinematographer Néstor Almendros takes magnificent advantage of the glorious natural light of the French Riviera, is a deceptively lovely film about less-than-lovely behavior, an ironic study of male acquisitiveness and priggish high-handedness in which two friends, a fastidious painter, Daniel (Pommereulle), and a dilettante art dealer, Adrien (Patrick Bauchau), find themselves sharing a summer house near Saint-Tropez with a third occupant, a young woman named Haydée Politoff, who winds up in the middle of their psychological gamesmanship. Written in collaboration with its three leads, this gold-hued depiction of moral rot may be the film in which Rohmer’s mature style first appears fully formed.

screenings.title: Millionaires' Express

screenings.title: Disclosure Day
screenings.description: If you found out we weren’t alone, if someone showed you, proved it to you, would that frighten you? This summer, the truth belongs to eight billion people. Spielberg’s latest sci-fi movie event, his first film since 2022’s The Fabelmans, returns to a legacy of grand, other-worldly, mysterious spectacle. Starring Emily Blunt (Oppenheimer), Josh O’Connor (Challengers), and Colin Firth (The King’s Speech), Disclosure Day thrills in the tense moment when the unknown becomes known.

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. screenings.title: 3 Women
screenings.description: Alongside his more touted multi-character panoramas, Altman also had a fondness for small-scale dramas investigating the complexities of female psychology, and of these none is greater than the ineffable 3 Women, which finds Shelley Duvall, Sissy Spacek, and Janice Rule thrown together at a health spa in the California desert that caters to the elderly. screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Stalking Chernobyl
screenings.description: After showcasing two of her documentaries last year, Spectacle is proud to host the New York City premiere of iara lee’s latest feature, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL. Throughout her prolific career as a cultural film essayist, iara lee intentionally sought out Indigenous voices in political peril. Inspired by her 2010 documentary and participation in the Gaza Freedom Flotilla, iara lee established the Cultures of Resistance Network to raise awareness of folks on the margins and the art they create. With lee’s latest, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL, we’re witnesses to the Sami people, an Indigenous group based in Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia. Undergoing constant oppression against imperial forces and racist colonialism, with one Sami man in particular hypothesizing, “Art could be a weapon”. A motivating mantra that sums up the essence of iara lee’s filmmaking ethos, Spectacle Theater will be screening this alongside two power-defying docs: K2 & THE INVISIBLE FOOTMEN and STALKING CHERNOBYL.

screenings.title: Dread Beat an Blood
screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... An amazing snapshot of the time of the pre-Brixton riots... This is so relevant a movie. That’s what makes it so good.” – Gilles Peterson, BBC “A fascinating document of LKJ in his time and place, touring with the sound systems, strolling through the market and visiting Tulse Hill schools, vividly capturing black British culture in a country on the cusp of Thatcherism, just a few months before the Brixton uprising.” – Stephen Troussé, Uncut “An invaluable document of Brixton, an area that was already at the front lines of the anti-racist struggle, the streets in which people would soon rise up in rebellion. That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... He’s now celebrated as one of this country’s most influential cultural commentators.” – BBC “A revolutionary poet for our times.” – Jacobin “The Poet Laureate of Black Britain.” – Paul Gilroy “The roots of hip-hop run deep, and among the deepest branches remains Linton Kwesi Johnson, the Jamaican-born, British-raised poet, writer, and performer often hailed as the father of dub poetry.” – David Browne, Rolling Stone

screenings.title: Rose of Nevada
screenings.description: 30 years after vanishing at sea, the eponymous fishing vessel mysteriously reappears in the harbor of a seaside village. The astonished local citizens see its return as a sign, convinced the luck of their economically devastated community may turn, if only the ship sails again. Joining the crew are Nick (George MacKay), desperate to provide for his young family, and Liam (Callum Turner), a mysterious drifter eager to escape his past. When they return from their voyage, nothing is as they remember it. Shooting in supersaturated color on a 16mm Bolex and constructing all the sound in post, Mark Jenkin’s hallucinatory time-travel mystery further solidifies him as one of the most singular artists working in film today.

His only ally is Navin (Joe Taslim) — a relentless journalist whose wife has mysteriously disappeared. Fueled by a furious vengeance, the unlikely duo ruthlessly fights against the kidnappers in this explosive martial arts showdown.

screenings.title: Collateral
screenings.description: Los Angeles cabbie Max Durocher (Jamie Foxx) is in for the toughest fare of his working life when he picks up one Vincent (Tom Cruise, natty in charcoal gray sharkskin suit), a jazz enthusiast and professional hitman who quite firmly insists that his driver accompany him on his evening’s rounds, leaving a trail of bodies in his wake. Shooting LA exteriors after dark with a then-state-of-the-art Sony F-900 digital camera, Mann gave his film a wholly distinctive texture—combining expressionistic smear with a new ability to pick up detail that would be lost on celluloid—and initiated a quiet revolution in low-light cinematography. A drum-tight character-based thriller, and the only film in which you can see Tom Cruise saying: “Yo, homie… Is that my briefcase?”

screenings.title: Julian
screenings.description: Fleur and Julian fall madly in love and decide to get married in all countries where they, as two women, are allowed to do so. But after only four marriages, their journey comes to a painful and unexpected halt.

screenings.title: Tampopo
screenings.description: Japanese milk-truck drivers (Tsutomu Yamazaki and Ken Watanabe) team up with the owner of a run-down roadside food stall (Nobuko Miyamoto, in the title role) to help her kick up her noodle-making game a notch in Itami’s brash, bawdy, knee-slapping “ramen Western,” a paean to the simple pleasures to be found at the kitchen table and in the boudoir.

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Agalmatophilia
screenings.description: Hollywood-sleaze auteur Jared Masters is an LA based, low budget filmmaker, creating an array of women-centric features inspired by VHS slashers and 60’s B-movies. His films represent a modern take on genre films, and have John Waters/Kuchar Brothers humor to them. Jared refers to himself as a modern cult filmmaker, occasionally starring in the films he makes. The three films selected are an introduction to his filmography, highlighting his taste for camp and self-aware humor, backed by a clear love for cinema. Masters works align with the Spectacle vision to highlight underrated, seldom-viewed filmmakers and late-night summer indies.

screenings.description: In this sweeping love story that spans three decades of passion, heartbreak and hope, Nino and Yasmina find themselves drawn together by a magnetic relationship. As they face an impossible choice between love and survival, they must decide if they want to build a family and chart a path to happiness in Lebanon, despite the tragedies ravaging the country. In Arabic with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: The Great Silence
screenings.description: The traditional slow-speaking taciturnity of the Western hero is taken to the extreme in Django director Corbucci’s hard-nosed, politically-provocative snowbound Spaghetti Western, set in turn-of-the-last-century Utah but filmed in the Italian Dolomites, where Jean-Louis Trintignant’s mute gunslinger has to face off against a band of outlaws led by Klaus Kinski at his most unhinged—and that’s saying something. According to no less a personage than Repo Man director and Spaghetti connoisseur Alex Cox, Corbucci’s “tightest, most relentless Western; his best and his bleakest.”

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

A wistful, winning, and quietly impassioned portrait of young love as it begins to bloom.

screenings.title: The Green Room
screenings.description: One of Truffaut’s most personal and beautiful films, photographed “in fecund greens and withering yellows” [Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader] by DP Néstor Almendros, and one of the least known of Truffaut’s major works—audiences, it seems, weren’t ready for this stark rumination on death from a filmmaker known for his gentle humor and twinkling personability. Truffaut, not far removed from his own premature end, stars himself alongside Nathalie Baye in this adaptation of Henry James’s short story “Altar of the Dead,” about a newspaper obituary writer who has become obsessed with the memory of friends departed from this mortal coil, represented here by images of the director’s own deceased loved ones.

The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

Already the pressure is on….

screenings.title: Club Lingerie
screenings.description: Hollywood-sleaze auteur Jared Masters is an LA based, low budget filmmaker, creating an array of women-centric features inspired by VHS slashers and 60’s B-movies. His films represent a modern take on genre films, and have John Waters/Kuchar Brothers humor to them. Jared refers to himself as a modern cult filmmaker, occasionally starring in the films he makes. The three films selected are an introduction to his filmography, highlighting his taste for camp and self-aware humor, backed by a clear love for cinema. Masters works align with the Spectacle vision to highlight underrated, seldom-viewed filmmakers and late-night summer indies.

screenings.title: Love in the Afternoon
screenings.description: The capstone entry of Rohmer’s Moral Tales series stars Bernard Verley as a happily married lawyer who assures us via voiceover that his wandering eye is in fact proof positive of his unshakable fidelity—but then his serene rectitude is tested sorely by the beguiling Chloé (Zouzou), a friend’s ex who becomes his confessor, his companion in empty afternoon hours, and a challenge to his very conception of himself. A film that casts a spell with little more than a few charismatic, unaffected performers, a shrewd, funny, pretense-puncturing script, and magisterial marshaling of natural light by cinematographer Néstor Almendros. “In its way, just about perfect.” —Pauline Kael, The New Yorker

screenings.title: The Red Light Bandit
screenings.description: Described by Sganzerla—21 years old when he directed his wild-eyed feature debut—as a “Western about the Third World,” The Red Light Bandit drew inspiration from the exploits of João Acácio Pereira da Costa, a recently arrested career criminal who’d acquired the status of folk hero, and, in its rough-edged style and vigorous montage, from the recent output of Jean-Luc Godard. A descent into the mean streets of São Paulo’s Boca do Lixo (Mouth of Garbage) neighborhood, Sganzerla’s brash, confrontational film is one of the key works of Brazil’s Cinema Marginal movement, per its creator: “Dirty and poetic, impure and pretentious… [speaking] of politics or of banditry without aesthetic respect, to the point of adopting an obscene liberty.”

screenings.title: The Misfits
screenings.description: Perhaps Huston’s most emotionally resonant film, an elegiac anti-western about a group of emotionally adrift people trying—and largely failing—to find connection in the modern American West. Written by Arthur Miller for his wife, Marilyn Monroe, at a time when their marriage was collapsing. The Misfits marked the last completed screen performances for both Monroe and Clark Gable. Another tragic Hollywood star, Montgomery Clift, also co-stars which adds to the film’s haunting metatextuality about damaged individuals and a dying way of life.

screenings.title: The Shooting
screenings.description: “Millie Perkins stars as an unnamed woman who hires two men – an ex-bounty hunter (Warren Oates) and his sidekick (Will Hitchins) – to take her through the desert on a mysterious revenge mission. The quest becomes more curious when a drifter (Jack Nicholson) begins to follow their trail. Written by Carole Eastman (FIVE EASY PIECES) and unofficially financed by Roger Corman, this film is less a revisionist Western and more a surreal, unsettling narrative set in the American West. screenings.title: Fallen Angels

Christopher Doyle’s cinematography has never been more woozily, blearily beautiful, nor has the Fragrant Harbor ever been put on screen with such transfixing nocturnal glamor.

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. screenings.description: Having proven himself a reliable hitmaker through the 1980s with Flashdance, 9½ Weeks, and Fatal Attraction, Lyne took an excursion into troubling new territory with this headlong plunge into the damaged psyche of Vietnam veteran Jacob Singer (Tim Robbins) who, haunted by his wartime experience and the death of a son, finds his drab daily life in c. 1975 New York City increasingly infringed on by nightmarish hallucinations—disturbing visions that suggest something more than run-of-the-mill PTSD. screenings.description: The debut feature from Jeong, one of a handful of female directors to break into the South Korean film industry, focuses on five young women, recent high school graduates living in the industrial port city of Incheon and facing a precarious future together, in addition to having to handle the practical exigencies of caring for the feline that they’ve communally adopted. Bae, whose Tae-hee makes ends meet with shifts at her family’s sauna and occasional work as a typist for a cerebral palsy-afflicted poet, anchors an exceedingly fine ensemble cast in Jeong’s moving drama of fraying friendships and economic uncertainty, also one of the first films to acknowledge the increasingly central role of text messaging in 21st-century communication and find a way to integrate this new, faceless form of “keeping in touch” into a filmed narrative.

screenings.title: The French Connection
screenings.description: “1971 was a hell of a year for gritty Big Apple movies... One of the best all-around tours of New York in [the 70s].” – Jason Bailey, Flavorwire “Hard-nosed, pork-pie-hatted, vulgar, a tough cop in the latest measure of a fine tradition, [Hackman] exists neither to rise nor to fall, to excite neither pity nor terror—but to function. To function in New York City is its own heroism, and the film recognizes that.” – The New York Times “A knockout police thriller with so much jarring excitement that it almost calls for comic-book expletives. POW! ZOWIE!” – Jay Cocks “Solid, slick filmmaking, full of dirty cops, shrewd operators, and slam-bang action.” – Dave Kehr “Like an aggravated case of New York.” – Pauline Kael “Friedkin’s symphony of long, sharp shocks is memorable for any number of sequences: the cat-and-mouse subway game, the ballbusting bar shakedown, a breakneck chase scene that still seems leagues ahead of greatest-ever competitors.” – David Fear, Time Out (New York) “Fraught with urban decay and racial tension, Friedkin’s bang-bang procedural created a paradigm for the tell-it-like-it-is cop drama... While Dirty Harry provided audiences an anti-establishment legal vigilante, THE FRENCH CONNECTION introduced the notion of the heroic working-class narc. Blue-collar to the bone, Popeye lives in public housing and feeds his face with a rancid-looking slice in the course of a freezing afternoon spent staking out on the Upper East Side boîte where the French smuggler who is about to unload 100 pounds of uncut heroin leisurely consumes a multi-course feast.” – J. Hoberman, The Village Voice “In a sense, the whole movie is a chase... the smugglers and the law officers are endlessly circling and sniffing each other… Doyle himself is a bad cop, by ordinary standards; he harasses and brutalizes people, he is a racist, he endangers innocent people during the chase scene (which is a high-speed ego trip)… THE FRENCH CONNECTION is as amoral as its hero, as violent, as obsessed and as frightening.” – Roger Ebert

screenings.title: The Flying Dutchman
screenings.description: “DEFA’s The Flying Dutchman is considered the first attempt to film a Wagner opera in its entirety, although, in point of fact, it too reworks the story to suit both the cinematic medium and the political viewpoint of the GDR. It was directed by opera director Joachim Herz, who, perhaps because it was his first (and only) film, opted to experiment with state-of-the-art sound and film techniques. Director Herz dramatically changes Wagner’s opera from one about a ghostly event to the reveries of a young woman named Senta who is infatuated with the story of the Flying Dutchman. To separate reality from Senta’s imagination, Mr. Herz uses two different film aspect ratios. Whenever we are watching Anna in the real world, the aspect ratio is [in 1.67:1]. When the film shifts to Senta’s dream world, the screen slowly opens up to the 2.35:1 dimensions of DEFA’s Totalvision (the same as Cinemascope). In other films that use multiple aspect ratios, the change in screen aspect is handled as edits, but Herz wanted these switches in perspective to flow like the film’s lush score. To do this required sophisticated in-camera techniques involving animation frames and an American Mitchell camera that accepted double reels. This process meant that everything had to be shot with the larger format while the animation frame was simultaneously running through the camera. That this worked at all is a testament to cinematographer Erich Gusko’s skill with a camera.” – Jim Morton

screenings.description: Perhaps Huston’s most emotionally resonant film, an elegiac anti-western about a group of emotionally adrift people trying—and largely failing—to find connection in the modern American West. Written by Arthur Miller for his wife, Marilyn Monroe, at a time when their marriage was collapsing. The Misfits marked the last completed screen performances for both Monroe and Clark Gable. Another tragic Hollywood star, Montgomery Clift, also co-stars which adds to the film’s haunting metatextuality about damaged individuals and a dying way of life.

screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... screenings.title: State of Grace
screenings.description: “His technique was almost invisible—you couldn’t even figure out if there was one… He understood everything about Jackie, how he’d behave and speak and move.” So said director Joanou of Gary Oldman’s loose-cannon performance in State of Grace, the actor’s US breakthrough, an inspired neo-noir that follows Terry Noonan (Sean Penn) on his return to Irish American Hell’s Kitchen after a long absence—unbeknownst to friends and neighbors now an undercover cop trying to take down a criminal organization whose members include Oldman’s Jackie Flannery and his elder brother, Frank (Ed Harris). Fervent admirers of Oldman’s work here include critic Roger Ebert, who praised “the twisted vision of [his] character, who lives in a world of evil and betrayal and has somehow thought himself around to the notion that he is doing the right thing,” and Leonardo DiCaprio, who stated that Oldman’s Jackie “influenced an entire generation of actors.”

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: El Topo
screenings.description: Chilean-born mime-turned-filmmaker Jodorowsky plays the title role in this acid Western staple of the midnight movies, strapping on the six-shooter as a lone gunfighter—his name means “The Mole” in Spanish—traveling across a psychedelic desert landscape on a quest to vanquish increasingly unusual villains while simultaneously confronting his own spiritual anguish and existential dread. A mind-melting trip through the doors of perception that counted John Lennon among its many acolytes, made up of “a phantasmagoric Mexican landscape laden with dead bunnies and burros, snarling hippie chicks, pregnant silences, buckets of blood, and guru-gunslingers.”—Manohla Dargis, The New York Times

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Game of Pleasure
screenings.description: Shot on video for the late-90s erotic-thriller market, GAME OF PLEASURE feels like a softcore Existenz for dummies. Writer/producer/star/co-editor Kevin Summerfield plays a hacker, stealing and selling games on the black market, and gets more than he bargained for when he stumbles on a new VR game called ‘Pleasure’, accidentally unleashing the horniest demon in DTV history (Home Shopping Network model turned adult film star Tammy Parks).

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: La Haine
screenings.description: A cinematic Molotov cocktail that was the first onscreen description of life (and death) in Paris’s banlieue housing projects that many French filmgoers had ever seen, La Haine depicts three armed and angry slum kids—Vincent Cassel, Hubert Koundé, and Saïd Taghmaoui—who, following days of rioting after the police’s savage beating of a young man, hit the city streets like ticking time bombs. A breakneck Steadicam journey through the concrete jungles of the suburbs, given an almost lunar desolation by the film’s black-and-white photography, La Haine is a propulsive, volatile, and visceral landmark of ’90s French cinema.

screenings.title: Happy Together

Winner of the Best Director prize at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, Wong’s Happy Together is a stunning display of filmmaking style and a touching story of love on the brink of dissolution.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. screenings.title: L'Argent
screenings.description: “In L’Argent I sense an unconditional surrender to despair and disgust. One can hardly argue that contemporary humanity does not deserve its full quotient of despair and disgust. And it is not even a matter of this social system or that. The rottenness seems to have plunged very deeply into the universal psyche. The artist, however is still obligated to search for order amid the chaos, for beauty amid the ugliness, for truth amid the falsehoods, and, above all, for hope amid the despair… That a filmmaker can lift us to these levels of contemplation and speculation is proof enough of that filmmaker’s greatness” —Andrew Sarris

screenings.title: Do You Love Me
screenings.description: A cinematic paean to Beirut and a journey into the collective audiovisual memory of Lebanon and its people, making use of film and television clips, home movies, and photographs drawn from private and public archives, materials spanning some 70 years of turbulent history. (Among the film’s parade of faces is that of director Jocelyne Saab, subject of a concurrent Metrograph series, visiting the wreckage of her former home, reduced to rubble in a 1982 Israeli air strike.) The glorious product of reclamation and meticulous research, and an urgent dispatch from an embattled nation, Do You Love Me proffers a people’s history that eschews linear chronology to offer instead a rich rhyming network of generation-crossing associations. A film of intimacy and alienation, of destruction and renewal, of grief and resilience.

screenings.description: The alpha and omega of conspiracy films, Stone’s deliriously entertaining cinematic inquest stars Kevin Costner as Jim Garrison, the New Orleans district attorney who came to find the circumstances of the 35th US president’s assassination more than a little fishy and got to digging around. Gary Oldman, as “patsy” Lee Harvey Oswald, stands out in a supporting cast teeming with familiar faces, including Tommy Lee Jones swishing it up as Louisiana businessman Clay Shaw, Brian Doyle-Murray as Jack Ruby, Donald Sutherland as whistleblower “Mr. X,” and Garrison himself as Justice Earl Warren. “A knockout. Part history book, part comic book, the movie rushes toward judgment for three breathless hours, lassoing facts and factoids by the thousands, then bundling them together into an incendiary device that would frag any viewer's complacency… Tip-top tabloid journalism. In its bravura and breadth, JFK is seditiously enthralling; in its craft, wondrously complex.” —Richard Corliss, Time

screenings.title: The Misfits

Written by Arthur Miller for his wife, Marilyn Monroe, at a time when their marriage was collapsing. The Misfits marked the last completed screen performances for both Monroe and Clark Gable. Another tragic Hollywood star, Montgomery Clift, also co-stars which adds to the film’s haunting metatextuality about damaged individuals and a dying way of life.

In Arabic with English subtitles.

In the company of his new friends, including the mysterious and mercurial Gloria (Lee of PAST LIVES), Ed has the uncanny feeling of merging with his younger self. Directed by Kent Jones (DIANE) from a witty, razor-sharp script by Samy Burch (MAY DECEMBER), LATE FAME is a funny, lively, poignant, and occasionally haunting New York story. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film 2025 96 MIN. USA MAGNOLIA PICTURES

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Maddie's Secret
screenings.description: Tuesday, June 16 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early Wednesday, June 17 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early and Carla Lalli Friday, June 19 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by John Wilson Friday, June 19 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Brace Belden Friday, June 19 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Ivy Wolk Friday, June 10 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early Saturday, June 20 at 11:30: Q&A with John Early moderated by Julio Torres Saturday, June 20 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Theda Hammel Saturday, June 20 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Sarah Sherman Saturday, June 20 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Amy Sedaris Saturday, June 20 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early

screenings.title: Barrio Triste
screenings.description: Medellin, 1987. A group of teen outcasts steals a news camera to document every detail of their dangerous lives. The first feature from acclaimed photographer and Bad Bunny music video director Stillz redefines the found footage genre as a haunting, poignant coming-of-age story with a disturbing twist. Set to an awe-inspiring score by Arca and produced by Harmony Korine’s collective EDGLRD, the film taps into the anxieties of a youth culture from the margins of history yearning to be understood.
screenings.country: Barrio Triste Crime, Drama, Fantasy, Horror

screenings.title: Dread Beat an Blood
screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... An amazing snapshot of the time of the pre-Brixton riots... This is so relevant a movie. That’s what makes it so good.” – Gilles Peterson, BBC “A fascinating document of LKJ in his time and place, touring with the sound systems, strolling through the market and visiting Tulse Hill schools, vividly capturing black British culture in a country on the cusp of Thatcherism, just a few months before the Brixton uprising.” – Stephen Troussé, Uncut “An invaluable document of Brixton, an area that was already at the front lines of the anti-racist struggle, the streets in which people would soon rise up in rebellion. That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... He’s now celebrated as one of this country’s most influential cultural commentators.” – BBC “A revolutionary poet for our times.” – Jacobin “The Poet Laureate of Black Britain.” – Paul Gilroy “The roots of hip-hop run deep, and among the deepest branches remains Linton Kwesi Johnson, the Jamaican-born, British-raised poet, writer, and performer often hailed as the father of dub poetry.” – David Browne, Rolling Stone

screenings.title: Julian
screenings.description: Fleur and Julian fall madly in love and decide to get married in all countries where they, as two women, are allowed to do so. But after only four marriages, their journey comes to a painful and unexpected halt.

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: The Sami Song of Survival
screenings.description: After showcasing two of her documentaries last year, Spectacle is proud to host the New York City premiere of iara lee’s latest feature, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL. Throughout her prolific career as a cultural film essayist, iara lee intentionally sought out Indigenous voices in political peril. Inspired by her 2010 documentary and participation in the Gaza Freedom Flotilla, iara lee established the Cultures of Resistance Network to raise awareness of folks on the margins and the art they create. With lee’s latest, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL, we’re witnesses to the Sami people, an Indigenous group based in Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia. Undergoing constant oppression against imperial forces and racist colonialism, with one Sami man in particular hypothesizing, “Art could be a weapon”. A motivating mantra that sums up the essence of iara lee’s filmmaking ethos, Spectacle Theater will be screening this alongside two power-defying docs: K2 & THE INVISIBLE FOOTMEN and STALKING CHERNOBYL.

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Train to Busan
screenings.description: Yeon Sang-ho’s global phenomenon TRAIN TO BUSAN arrives back in theaters to celebrate its 10th Anniversary. What begins as a simple birthday trip for a father and daughter turns into a high-octane fight for survival when a zombie outbreak ravages South Korea. Trapped on a speeding train, they must navigate a landscape of terror to reach safety. Experience the relentless action and heart-wrenching drama on the big screen like never before.

screenings.title: Les Bonnes Femmes
screenings.description: An early and enormous artistic triumph of the French New Wave, Chabrol’s quietly class-conscious film records the dreams, dramas, and self-deceptions of a quartet of young Parisian girls working at an appliance shop, among them Bernadette Lafont and Stéphane Audran. A study of the social habits of the petite bourgeoisie, set against indubitably authentic locations seen in crisp black-and-white courtesy DP Henri Decaë, which develops into a melancholy cautionary tale on the risks of romantic illusion.

screenings.title: The Warriors
screenings.description: “Waaarriors! Come out and play-ay!” Falsely accused of responsibility for the assassination of New York’s most powerful ganglord during a citywide summit in the Bronx’s Van Cortlandt Park, Swan (Michael Beck) and his fellow Warriors now have to fight their way back, block by block and mano a mano, to the safe shores of their Coney Island turf. The film’s knuckle-busting action choreography and its vision of NYC as a coliseum-like proving grounds for epic heroism—its source, at a distance, is Xenophon’s 4th century BC Anabasis—are delectable, but its greatness lies in its attention to character, how it lets us see a crew of provincial Brooklynites gradually discovering they’re the toughest dudes in town.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. A MUSIC BOX FILMS RELEASE Open Caption (OC) Screenings Tuesday, July 28, 3:20 show Saturday, August 1, 3:20 show Sunday, August 2, 3:20 show Monday, August 3, 6:40 show Tuesday, August 4, 3:20 show

screenings.title: La Notte
screenings.description: Novelist Giovanni Pontano (Marcello Mastroianni) is the toast of the Italian literary scene, but smothered by the trappings of success. His misery weighs heavily on his wife, Lidia (Jeanne Moreau), already carrying her own cargo of existential anguish. In the course of a day and a night—spent at a hospital sickroom, a book launch, a nightclub, and a party at an industrialist’s villa, where Giovanni flirts extensively with the host’s daughter, Valentina (Monica Vitti)—the couple must come to terms with the extinction of the love that once existed between them… or not? A film steeped in despair but thrilling in its adventurous, architectonic use of the cinematic medium, from its opening credits—an avant-jazz/musique concrète overture accompanying the industrialized Milanese cityscape—to its beguiling final scene.

screenings.title: Disclosure Day
screenings.description: If you found out we weren’t alone, if someone showed you, proved it to you, would that frighten you? This summer, the truth belongs to eight billion people. Spielberg’s latest sci-fi movie event, his first film since 2022’s The Fabelmans, returns to a legacy of grand, other-worldly, mysterious spectacle. Starring Emily Blunt (Oppenheimer), Josh O’Connor (Challengers), and Colin Firth (The King’s Speech), Disclosure Day thrills in the tense moment when the unknown becomes known.

screenings.title: Deliverance
screenings.description: A quartet of city slicker businessman buddies (Jon Voight, Ned Beatty, Ronny Cox and, in a star-making role, Burt Reynolds) leave Atlanta to head into the Georgia backwoods for what’s meant to be a little weekend canoe trip… and stumble headlong instead into the hidden horrors lurking in the old Southland. The trial-by-fire endurance test that they’ll pass through makes for pure, pulse-pounding cinema, with at least three scenes—the “Dueling Banjos” gas station stop, Beatty’s “Squeal like a pig!” humiliation, and the white-water rapids set piece—that rank above the most remembered in ’70s American cinema.
